title: Lead Time and Early Warning Markers of Closure in US Hospitals, 2011–2023
content: Objective. To determine how many years before closure each financial and operational marker becomes visible in critical access hospitals, the category of small rural facility that United States policy protects through cost-based Medicare reimbursement. Methods. Medicare cost reports for federal fiscal years 2011 to 2023 were restricted to critical access hospitals and to reports covering 150 to 366 inclusive days, giving 17 425 hospital-years from 1423 facilities in 45 states. Five overlapping samples were constructed in which the outcome was cessation of cost-report filing exactly one, two, three, four or five years after the observation year. For each of 15 markers an adjusted odds ratio per standard deviation was estimated with year indicators, adjustment for size and ownership, and standard errors clustered by hospital. Discrimination was summarized by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with bootstrap intervals. Results. Closure was visible well in advance. Liquidity carried the signal at every horizon: the current ratio was associated with closure from one to five years ahead (odds ratios 0.31, 0.38, 0.45, 0.40 and 0.50 per standard deviation), and days cash on hand was the single strongest marker at one year (0.22 (95% CI 0.09–0.55)). Total margin was associated with closure from one to four years. Size and occupancy carried little information, and no association with size reached significance at any horizon. Discrimination fell only modestly, from 0.883 (95% CI 0.832–0.929) at one year to 0.784 (0.680–0.867) at five. Conclusions. In critical access hospitals the earliest and most persistent warning sign is liquidity rather than the structural measures that dominate analyses of hospitals in general. Monitoring frameworks applied to this category should weight cash and the current ratio accordingly. Estimates rest on 37 closures at one year and 19 at five and are correspondingly imprecise.
